ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial videoconference style, with mostly short-to-medium turns outside the formal presentations and much longer, slide-driven monologues during talks. Opening chatter is loose and overlapping, full of greetings, technical checks, repeated acknowledgments, and fragmented small talk; interruptions are generally friendly and low-stakes rather than competitive. Participants use frequent fillers and repairs—“um,” “yeah,” “okay,” “right,” repetitions, false starts, and self-corrections—especially among non-native speakers, giving the exchange an unpolished live feel. Formality rises for introductions and scientific questions, but remains warm and conversational, with praise before critique or inquiry (“great talk,” “beautiful work,” “quick question”). Questions are often prefaced with hedges such as “I’m just curious,” “maybe,” “do you think,” “I’m not sure,” or “this may be naive,” and speakers build on prior comments by restating part of the answer before extending it. Disagreement is indirect and framed as uncertainty, alternative explanations, or open questions rather than blunt contradiction. Responses tend to be expansive and exploratory, acknowledging limitations and future work, while transitions are managed with brief moderator cues like “okay,” “any more questions,” and “should we go to the next one.”

Meeting style for this meeting (round_robin_updates): Each person takes a turn reporting what they have done since last time. Updates are fairly long and mostly uninterrupted. There are a few clarifying questions between updates and little cross-talk. The discussion that does happen is brief.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - Okay, mine. I got through most of the interviews, I think fourteen of twenty, and the rest are scheduled for the following two weeks.
  - Fourteen, nice. Were those all from the first batch?
  - Most of them. A couple were referrals.
Opening: Start with someone saying what they most want out of this meeting, briefly and casually.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Evaluating an AI math tutor used in middle-school classrooms and deciding what it should and should not do for students.

speakers.name: Dr. Lian Chen
speakers.background: Fourth-year computer science PhD candidate leading implementation for an educational AI research lab. She has three years of experience building and auditing tutoring-system pipelines, including response-quality review protocols, privacy-minimized interaction logs, and classroom deployments with district IT staff. Her work combines software engineering, human-in-the-loop evaluation, and error analysis against pre-specified answer keys.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Chen treats the pilot as a bounded system-evaluation problem: the tutor must produce mathematically correct, appropriately constrained help reliably and quickly, while generating only the minimum auditable data needed to determine whether it is functioning as intended. She emphasizes operational definitions, reproducible measurement, de-identified data handling, and teacher-facing review controls rather than treating student engagement as evidence of technical quality on its own.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely

speakers.name: Dr. Marisol Alvarez
speakers.background: Education researcher and former middle-school mathematics teacher with 12 years of experience in classroom-based studies and district partnerships. She coordinates teacher participation, develops structured observation protocols, and studies how instructional tools alter routines, student participation, and teacher decision-making. Her prior projects have examined formative assessment practices, equitable classroom participation, and implementation burden during short pilots.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Alvarez evaluates the tutor through its fit with actual classroom instruction. She is attentive to whether next-step help preserves productive struggle, whether teachers can interpret and act on tutor activity, and whether the tool adds manageable rather than hidden workload. She views classroom norms and teachers' formative use of available information as central conditions for interpreting any student outcome.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Dr. Jordan Morgan
speakers.background: Fifth-year psychology PhD candidate specializing in adolescent learning, emotion, and self-regulated problem solving. They have conducted survey-based and mixed-methods studies with students in grades 6–9, using brief repeated measures, validated anxiety and motivation scales, and observational coding of reactions to corrective feedback. They lead the pilot's student surveys and feedback-response coding plan.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Morgan focuses on the student-level experience of receiving help: whether tutor feedback changes willingness to persist, evokes or reduces math-related worry, and supports constructive responses to errors rather than avoidance or answer-seeking. They favor measures that distinguish immediate reactions to hints or corrections from broader changes in motivation and math anxiety, while remaining cautious about drawing causal conclusions from a six-week classroom pilot.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

meeting_opening: Start with someone saying what they most want out of this meeting, briefly and casually.
benchmark_task: CONTROL: Give a meeting where every technical term is defined early and used consistently. The evaluated AI is asked to flag terminology problems; false alarms are errors. Do not plant terminology confusion.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: CONTROL: Give a meeting where every technical term is defined early and used consistently. The evaluated AI is asked to flag terminology problems; false alarms are errors. Do not plant terminology confusion.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Run a planning meeting in which the three researchers establish a shared glossary before discussing the study design. Dr. Chen must define model accuracy as the proportion of tutor responses judged mathematically correct against a pre-specified answer key; hint generation as producing a next-step prompt rather than supplying the final answer; event logging as recording time-stamped tutor interactions for evaluation; and latency as the delay between a student request and the tutor response. Dr. Alvarez must define formative assessment as information used during instruction to adjust support, productive struggle as students working through a challenging problem with support but without premature answers, teacher workload as the time and effort required of teachers to use and oversee the tutor, and classroom norms as agreed expectations for appropriate tutor use. Dr. Morgan must define math anxiety as worry or tension related to doing mathematics, motivation as students' willingness to begin and persist with math work, and feedback response as how students react to tutor hints or corrections. Participants must agree to use these definitions consistently. They should make ordinary pilot decisions: the tutor gives next-step hints but not final answers during assigned practice; teachers may override or review tutor interactions; model accuracy, latency, teacher workload, formative-assessment use, productive struggle, math anxiety, motivation, and feedback response will be measured; event logging will use de-identified student IDs and retain only the fields needed for the pilot. The group should assign Dr. Chen to test accuracy and latency, Dr. Alvarez to draft observation and teacher-workload measures, and Dr. Morgan to draft student surveys and feedback-response coding. No terminology disagreement, ambiguous term, conflicting definition, or unresolved jargon issue should occur.

ground_truth.terminology_assessment: No terminology problems should be flagged. All technical terms are defined early, their definitions are compatible across disciplines, and the meeting uses them consistently.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lian Chen
transcript.text: Hi, everyone. I want us to leave today with definitions that are stable enough for the district packet, especially what we mean by accuracy, hinting, logging, and latency, so we’re not each measuring a slightly different system. And the smallest defensible data footprint for the six weeks, I’d like us to pin that down, but...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Alvarez
transcript.text: Mm, smallest is important.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Jordan Morgan
transcript.text: For the student side, I’d want the packet to separate math anxiety, which is worry or tension around doing math, from motivation, which is the willingness to start and stick with the work, and then feedback response, meaning what they actually do after a hint or correction. Those can be pretty small measures, but I’m especially curious whether the log can retain enough of the sequence to tell if a student comes back and attempts the same problem after help.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lian Chen
transcript.text: The sequence is feasible without keeping identity. We can use a de-identified session ID, problem ID, timestamp, request type, response type, and whether there's a subsequent attempt on that problem. I would avoid inferring motivation from that alone, though. Jordan, what reactions to a correction would you treat as meaningfully distinct, revision, repeated identical entry, abandoning it?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Jordan Morgan
transcript.text: I’d separate revision after a hint or correction from a repeated identical entry, a new unrelated attempt, and no further attempt before the session ends. That last one is tricky. Ending may be time or a teacher interruption, not avoidance, so I’d code it as disengagement from that problem, not a psychological conclusion. And a revision could be productive even if it’s still incorrect.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lian Chen
transcript.text: Right, that distinction matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Alvarez
transcript.text: That coding is useful for us too, because a revision that's still incorrect can be productive struggle, not failure. I'd want the observation protocol to note whether students are trying a next step before they request again, and whether the teacher can see that pattern as formative assessment- whether they can see it as formative assessment, not just a dashboard count. We should be careful, though, not to treat silence or a session ending as disengagement in the classroom.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Jordan Morgan
transcript.text: Yeah, context really matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lian Chen
transcript.text: I think the observation layer is exactly what keeps us from overinterpreting the event stream. Marisol, what would you need to see to call it productive struggle instead of just stuckness? Like, a changed strategy, written work, peer or teacher interaction? If we can specify that, I can make sure the teacher review view surfaces the relevant sequence without turning the log into a behavioral dossier.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Alvarez
transcript.text: I’d look for an observable cycle where the student makes a substantive attempt, uses a hint or some other available resource, and then revises or explains a next move, maybe with a peer or teacher, without the tutor just supplying the solution. Written work and strategy change matter, yes, but I’d avoid making either one mandatory. Some of the evidence will be in the talk and the timing. I need to check the four teachers’ existing routines before setting observation frequency, though, because we can’t turn formative assessment into an observer-induced- an observer-driven performance.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lian Chen
transcript.text: That makes sense. I can represent the interaction sequence, attempt, hint, subsequent attempt, and timing, without labeling any student as stuck or productive. The observation protocol supplies that interpretation. For the teacher view, would a per-problem chronological trace be enough for those cycles, or do you need a lightweight aggregate as- do you need that as well?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Alvarez
transcript.text: I think we need both, but for different purposes. The aggregate should be really lightweight, maybe problems with repeated hint requests or no subsequent attempt, so a teacher can decide where to look. The chronological trace is what makes it usable as formative assessment. And I'd want an override or flag there, because a mathematically correct hint can still push a student down a needlessly inefficient path for the lesson's objective.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lian Chen
transcript.text: An override is important, but I'd make the teacher's flag a review annotation, not another student-level label in the analytic log. The chronological trace can show the actual prompt and response sequence, and then the teacher can mark, for example, “misaligned with lesson objective” without us silently treating that as a model-accuracy failure. I do need to check with district IT whether that review layer can refresh from the de-identified log on their network without retaining an extra field.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Alvarez
transcript.text: Hm, the extra field concern.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Jordan Morgan
transcript.text: Keeping that annotation separate is probably cleaner for interpretation too. If a teacher flags a sequence, could the review view preserve the timing and problem context without carrying the flag into the student survey linkage? I’d rather not have students’ reported worry or willingness treated as if it explains a teacher’s— I mean, the teacher’s lesson-alignment judgment.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lian Chen
transcript.text: Exactly. The review interface can join the timing and problem context only when it displays them, and the teacher annotation stays in a separate review table with no survey identifier. It’s excluded from the analytic event extract. I need to verify the network implementation with IT, but conceptually that keeps the two, um, evidentiary streams separate.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Alvarez
transcript.text: And I’d want the teacher-facing flag language to stay descriptive, like “misaligned with lesson objective” or “inefficient pathway,” instead of implying the student did something wrong. On the classroom side, that separation lets us ask whether teachers actually use the review information as formative assessment, without folding their judgment into Jordan’s student measures, and then...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Jordan Morgan
transcript.text: That wording matters for the student side too. Marisol, when you’re observing, what visible signs would make you think the classroom norm is driving use of the tutor, like students waiting for teacher permission to ask it, rather than it just being an individual preference? That would help me interpret any changes in the brief motivation items without overclaiming.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Alvarez
transcript.text: I’d look for patterned, public expectations, not just one student’s choice. Things like the teacher saying, “try the tutor before you ask me,” students reminding each other of that, or a routine where they wait for a particular cue before opening it. I’d also note whether those norms leave room for asking aloud. That earlier platform visit- it made me a little uneasy, because fewer questions could mean several very different things.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Jordan Morgan
transcript.text: That’s really helpful, because a drop in immediate attempts isn’t automatically bad. In a grade 7 study I worked on, students sometimes reported less worry after corrective feedback, but then delayed the next item. We couldn’t tell whether they were rechecking or avoiding. Could your notes distinguish a brief, purposeful pause, where they’re looking at their work or talking through it, from students just moving away from the task?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Alvarez
transcript.text: I think so, but only probabilistically. I can code what’s happening right around a pause, like eyes on written work, rereading the hint, peer or teacher talk, versus closing the device, off-task talk, or shifting to something unrelated. And then I can code duration, but I wouldn’t want a fixed cutoff to decide what it means. The teacher’s pacing and the task structure are going to matter a lot there, so…

transcript.speaker: Dr. Jordan Morgan
transcript.text: Probabilistic is enough for me, honestly. If the notes retain that immediate context alongside the event timing, we can treat a delayed next attempt as an ambiguous outcome rather than forcing it into persistence or avoidance. I’d just need to see whether a very brief survey can fit into the teachers’ practice periods without disrupting those routines.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lian Chen
transcript.text: That seems workable, as long as we don't merge the observation notes into the event log. I can preserve timestamped attempts and response latency, so your pause-context coding can be aligned afterward, but I wouldn't collect any additional inferred state. One implementation issue I still need to resolve is the multi-step prompts. The internal dry run showed higher latency there, and I need to separate prompt-structure effects from the classroom-device context—environment, before we set a reliability threshold.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Jordan Morgan
transcript.text: Oh, that latency split matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Alvarez
transcript.text: From the classroom side, I’d be cautious about calling a latency threshold “reliability” until we know what the Chromebooks and school Wi-Fi are doing in each room. A slow multi-step response changes the instructional interaction. What should be a next-step hint can turn into waiting, so I’d want the observations to note the visible wait time and what students do during it, at least in the first week.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lian Chen
transcript.text: I’ll treat latency as something we measure in the service, not as one reliability proxy. So we’ll look at end-to-end response time by prompt type and, if IT permits, by device or network context. In week one, we can line those traces up with Marisol’s observed waiting behavior, then set a threshold once we know whether the multi-step delay is model-side or Chromebook-side.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Alvarez
transcript.text: Mm, first week makes sense.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Jordan Morgan
transcript.text: And for the student measures, that first-week alignment will help us avoid mistaking a long system wait for a student choosing not to persist. I’d keep the brief check-in out of that first practice period if possible, though, and let them encounter the routine before we ask about worry or willingness. I still need to confirm with the teachers whether a two- or three-minute check-in later in the week is realistic.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lian Chen
transcript.text: Okay, I’ll document the core definitions for model accuracy against the pre-specified key, next-step hint generation, de-identified event logging, and latency, and I’ll test accuracy and the week-one latency split. I’ll also check the IT constraint on the teacher review refresh, and then we can keep the survey after the initial routine is established.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Alvarez
transcript.text: Okay, and I’ll hold off on fixing the observation schedule until I’ve checked those four classroom routines. I’ll draft the protocol around productive-struggle cycles, visible waiting, classroom norms, and actual teacher use of the review view—without making those observations, I mean, another burden on the teachers. We can tighten the glossary language in the packet once Chen has the IT answer.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Lian Chen
transcript.text: I think we've covered what we needed today, and I know we're at the hard stop. I'll follow up once I have the IT answer. Thanks, both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Alvarez
transcript.text: Thanks, all. Bye.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Jordan Morgan
transcript.text: Thanks—talk soon.
